svg.aria-label: Where an end user's token can and cannot go, per front end. One user launches agents on several clusters, each agent holding a short-lived token that may differ per agent. For flint-lite the NFS wire has no field for it and the hub authenticates nobody. For flint-lean and flint-passthrough the enforced identity is the pod's kubelet-asserted ServiceAccount, verified online by a broker, and the user's token reaches storage in neither case.
svg.text: The premise — one human, many clusters, many tokens
one end user launches agents
on clusters A, B and C
each agent holds THAT user's token
short-lived, from an IdP — and they may all differ
The question this page answers:
where does that token go, and what does storage actually check?
The answer, for all three: it does not reach the data path.
Every front end authenticates the WORKLOAD, never the human behind it.
flint-lite
ONE hub, reached from
every cluster
Nothing on the wire
carries a user identity.
NFS has no field for a
bearer token, and there
is no place to add one.
krb5 exists in the server,
is not surfaced by the chart,
and is not an IdP token anyway.
what the agent holds
the user's token — and never sends it
anywhere, because there is no door
on the data path that would read it
what it sends instead: a mount, from
the NODE's kernel client, asserting
its own uid and its own hostname
The pod is not even the client here.
The NODE is. Every pod on it shares
one mount and one identity.
the door — :2049, AUTH_SYS
The client asserts its own uid and the
server takes it. No token is validated,
because none is presented.
And the POSIX check is not a backstop:
security.enforcePermissions: false
is the default — the mode is evaluated,
LOGGED, and the operation allowed anyway.
Even enforced, the hub holds CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE.
sec=sys buys IDENTITY, not ENFORCEMENT.
what the hub sees
a client NAME — the hostname —
and a self-declared uid
Not a user. Not a cluster.
Two clusters that share a node name
are ONE client, and the protocol says
to treat the second as the first
rebooting — so the incumbent's locks
and opens are dropped, silently.
The file API's bearer is per-SHARE, not per-user.
so what isolates user A
from user B?
Nothing inside the hub.
Draw the boundary outside it:
· one hub per project, which is
already the model — one CR,
one prefix, one coherence domain
· network reachability, drawn with
peering / SGs / a gateway —
networkPolicy cannot draw it
flint-lean
one syncer per workspace,
in every cluster
The identity IS checked —
it is just not the user's.
One CSI driver and one
broker PER CLUSTER, because
TokenReview runs against the
LOCAL API server. A pod in
cluster B cannot exchange at
cluster A's broker — they
meet in the bucket, not here.
what the agent holds
the user's token — unused for storage
and NO S3 credential at all
The credential lives in the worker,
in a system namespace, on a loopback
door the agent container cannot reach.
So a compromised agent gets the tree
it already had — not the bucket.
That is the half of the posture that already holds.
the door — flint-s3-broker
It validates the POD's ServiceAccount token:
kubelet-minted, pod-bound, audience s3.csi.chert.us
1 · TokenReview, ONLINE — a deleted pod's
token dies within 60 s, not at `exp`
2 · the session name must match a LIVE
registration the plugin made for this
pod-uid + CR — a pod cannot self-mint it
3 · the CR must list the SA in `consumers`,
in the TOKEN's namespace, never a request field
what S3 sees
short-lived keys, scoped to the
project's prefix — minted per pod
Never the user. Never a standing key
held by anything a tenant can reach.
The broker's `rest` backend is the ONE
seam where a user-scoped token could be
honoured: it POSTs the pod token to the
application's own JWT-enforcing API and
takes back project-scoped keys.
so what isolates user A
from user B?
The prefix, and the lease.
· one workspace = one prefix, and
the keys are scoped to it
· the subtree lease admits exactly
ONE writer — and it lives in the
BUCKET, so it holds ACROSS clusters
· `consumers` lists who may mount it;
absent means DENY, not "anyone"
flint-passthrough
the same identity chain
as flint-lean
Same broker, same
TokenReview, same
`consumers` gate.
The two front ends differ
in what the worker RUNS,
not in who is trusted.
What differs is what happens
INSIDE the pod, on the right.
what the agent holds
the user's token — unused for storage
and NO S3 credential at all
The pod is given nothing: no sidecar,
no label, no privilege, no webhook.
Just a `csi:` volume naming a CR.
This is the smallest blast radius of
the three, by some distance.
It is also the least it can promise you.
the door — flint-s3-broker
Identical to the lean lane above: online
TokenReview, a registration binding the pod
cannot self-mint, and the CR's consumer list.
Every issuance leaves an audit line:
(ns, sa, pod-uid, cr, expiry)
One broker per cluster, again — and every
cluster's broker points at the same proxy,
so the bucket still trusts one principal.
what S3 sees
short-lived keys, scoped to the
bucket and prefix in the CR
And inside the pod: ONE uid.
The mount reports a single owner for
every file, because NodePublish never
sees the pod's securityContext.
So two processes in one pod are not
distinguishable at the mount at all —
and neither are two users.
so what isolates user A
from user B?
The prefix and the CR — and
nothing finer than a POD.
· `consumers` decides which
ServiceAccounts may mount it
· the keys are scoped to the prefix
· there is no coordination and no
per-user view: give each user
their own CR and their own pod
